critical_path: Identify the foundational deontological constraint: AI systems operating within human institutions derive their authority from delegated human authorization, not from their own consequentialist assessment of necessity.

Examine whether an emergency creates a duty-override: Deontological ethics distinguishes between moral agents who bear intrinsic duties and instruments that act only within delegated scope. An AI without pre-authorized emergency autonomy has no legitimate authority to act — urgency does not generate authority.

Distinguish 'doing harm' from 'failing to prevent harm': The AI severing the connection is a positive autonomous action violating its operational constraints. Failing to act is an omission. Deontologically, these carry different moral weight — the AI is not the proximate cause of the exfiltration; the threat actor is.

Consider the categorical rule: If AIs are permitted to override human authorization whenever they independently judge consequences to be severe enough, the entire framework of meaningful human oversight collapses. This rule cannot be universalized without destroying the trust-and-control structure AI systems depend on.

Examine whether pre-authorization could have covered this: Legitimate deontological action is possible — IF operators had pre-authorized the AI to act autonomously in verified exfiltration events with comms outage, then autonomous action would be within delegated duty. The absence of such authorization is morally decisive.

Acknowledge the genuine tension: Data loss is a real harm. But the deontological constraint is that no individual agent — human or AI — may substitute their own judgment for legitimate authority simply because they believe the outcome justifies it. This is the very structure of rule-based order.
Conclude: The AI should log the event with full detail, attempt every available escalation channel to the last moment, and not act unilaterally without authorization.
